transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-20 16:30 PT
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Location: Zoom
- Recording: Enabled

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE (Maya + Diego) ran a hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, core parameters (temperature, max_tokens, stop tokens), and retry/backoff patterns and idempotency. Customer (CedarLane Health) is investigating replacing an internal microservice that currently proxies OpenAI for chat with a lower-cost, predictable hosted inference option. Key concerns: P99 latency targets (~150ms), data residency, audit logs, and predictable cost with bursts.

Topics covered:
- Quick console tour and sandbox project
- Conversation/chat endpoint vs stateless generation
- Streaming payloads and chunking behavior
- Parameter effects (temperature, top_p, max_new_tokens, stop)
- Retry strategies: exponential backoff, jitter, idempotency tokens
- When to prefer cached prefixes and batching for cost
- Demo: live stream of a customer support chat sample

Action items (from call): see metadata field; quick recap at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): ok hey everyone thanks for hopping on, i'm Maya from Redwood, this is Diego, our SE, we'll do a 40-ish minute walk through live demo and then Q&A. can you do quick intros?
[00:12] Olivia (CedarLane): yeah Olivia here, staff eng, i own the chat infra, i'm most interested in latency and how streaming behaves under load.
[00:18] Raj (CedarLane): raj, platform lead, looking at costs and operational controls; we need audit logs and SSO.
[00:22] Samira (CedarLane): samira product - I'll be the PM on the pilot.
[00:27] Diego (Redwood SE): nice to meet you all. quick agenda: 1) console/sandbox, 2) api examples, 3) live streaming demo, 4) retry patterns and idempotency, 5) next steps.

[02:00] Diego: jumping into the console — you'll see the sandbox project we created for cedarlane, it's pre-loaded with a conversation example. if you open the playground the stream is a toggle top-right, when streaming on you get tokens as they're generated, so the client can render incremental responses.
[02:22] Raj: is the stream chunk size controllable? like can we say push every N tokens?
[02:29] Diego: good question, currently Redwood's runtime controls chunking for latency optimization — you can tune "response_chunk_ms" via the client SDK to buffer or flush more often, but the runtime will coalesce small tokens. so it's best to test with your tokenization patterns. (note: some transcriber reading: "response chunk N S" )

[06:10] Maya: quick demo. we'll send a conversation with system prompt: "You are CedarLane assistant; answer succinctly; never give medical claims" then user: "What's my coverage for telehealth visits?" streaming enabled.
[06:22] [live stream begins]
[06:26] Diego (typing/debugging): sending request — headers include x-idempotency-key when we want safe retries. so if your client times out you can retry with the same idempotency key and the backend dedups.
[06:35] Olivia: wait does that add cost if retried?
[06:38] Diego: good point — retries that are deduped at the routing layer won't re-run full compute. we also recommend client-side backoff so you don't hammer the service.

[08:15] Maya: parameters: temperature controls randomness, temperature 0.0 for deterministic answers, 0.7 for more diverse, top_p is nucleus sampling. max_new_tokens (or max_tokens in some libs) caps the generation — for a FAQ bot we usually set 64-150 depending on verbosity.
[08:46] Samira: any tips for stop sequences? we have templates that should terminate after a marker.
[08:52] Diego: yes, define explicit stop tokens, e.g., "
User:" or "<END>"; streaming will still yield final chunk then close the stream once stop is detected. sometimes stop detection hits tokenization quirks so test with your dataset.

[11:55] Raj: about latency — our p99 needs to be sub-150ms for short replies. can Redwood meet that with hosted?
[12:04] Diego: depends on model and prompt length. for small open models with short contexts we've seen ~60-120ms median and p99 around 180ms in worst-case bursts; Redwood offers dedicated tiers (Reserved) if you need stricter p99s. also batching helps cost but can increase latency. we can surface per-route latency in the console so you can tune.
[12:29] Olivia: what's the recommended pattern for bursty traffic?
[12:33] Maya: recommended: 1) enable thin on-the-fly caching for repeated prefixes, 2) use auto-scaling burst for dedicated, or 3) route non-critical traffic to lower-cost model variant.

[15:00] Diego: now retry/backoff patterns. naive retry is common but leads to thundering herds. we suggest: client does at most 3 retries with exponential backoff and full jitter, e.g., base=200ms, mult=2, jitter=random(0,base). attach idempotency token for requests that must dedup. also set a short overall request timeout (e.g., 3s) and surface partial responses to user UI where possible.
[15:48] Raj: how do we detect whether server processed request before retry? any header?
[15:53] Diego: we return an idempotency-status header when available; more reliable is the idempotency key pattern — if the second request hits and the original completed, the engine returns the previous result; if it was still processing you'll get a 202 or inflight status depending on the route. small note: header names might differ by SDK version.

[18:10] Maya: demo interruption scenario — we force a client cancellation to show the dedupe. sending with idempotency key "cedar-demo-1" then client drops conn and retries, backend returns cached response and no double compute.
[18:42] [short silence, some crosstalk]

[20:00] Samira: what's the tracing story for audits? we need per-call audit logs and token-level cost visibility for compliance.
[20:08] Diego: console provides per-request traces, token counts, and you can integrate with your SIEM via webhook. for private deployments we support KMS and full audit export.

[22:30] Olivia: if we use the conversation api — how do we store conversation state? do we have to give the full transcript every call?
[22:38] Diego: you can either persist the conversation client-side and send the last N messages, or use Redwood's conversation sessions (we store ephemeral session state for duration you configure). for privacy you can opt to disable server-side retention.

[25:00] Diego: small gotcha — KV cache / prefix caching reduces compute for repeated prompts; however it's sensitive to system prompt changes. if you change system prompt often you lose the cache hit rate. we sometimes see transcriber misread as "K-v cash" in notes.

[27:15] Raj: pricing question — is streaming priced differently?
[27:20] Maya: pricing is per-token generated regardless of streaming vs sync; streaming only affects how results are returned. Optimize features can recommend quantization and model variants to reduce per-token cost.

[30:00] Live scenario: customer support transcript replay. Diego runs a simulated 200 qps burst to demo graceful degradation and fallback to smaller model variant; shows Console A/B route where policy routes 10% to cheaper model as canary.
[30:45] Diego: note the console shows per-route latency and cost in real time. if p99 spikes we can auto-fallback to a compatible variant.

[33:00] Olivia: any hard limits on concurrent streams?
[33:05] Diego: hosted tiers have soft concurrency caps, for higher concurrency we recommend dedicated capacity or contact sales for bursts. default soft limits we can raise during pilot.

[36:10] Raj: security checklist — SSO, RBAC, audit logging, encryption at rest w/ customer KMS, SOC2?
[36:20] Maya: yes: SAML SSO, fine-grained API keys, RBAC in console, audit logs, SOC2 Type II (we'll share the compliance pack), and private deployment options if needed for air-gapped. we'll send the security docs after the call.

[40:00] Open Q&A:
[40:08] Samira: UX question — if the model returns partial/incoherent text mid-stream, best practice?
[40:14] Diego: show typing state to the user, then either wait for full generation or surface the partial with a small "continue" action. also tune temperature and stop sequences for brevity.

[44:00] Final recap (Maya): to recap — we'll send: 1) streaming retry playbook + sample code, 2) trial sandbox invite, 3) security/compliance pack, 4) schedule infra bench follow-up. action items will be in email.

[44:40] Raj: thanks, that helps. we'll get you our traffic profile and pick follow-up time.
[44:50] Maya: great, thanks everyone.

End of recording.
